title: Women of Prairie Avenue
premise: A spring morning walk past six houses tied to women who changed Chicago: nursing, forensic science, a forty-year journal, suffrage, a famous fountain and the street's last great lady.

opening.text:
JAUNT: WOMEN OF PRAIRIE AVENUE. A spring morning, 1904. The men of this street have gone downtown to their stores, banks and packing houses, and their names are on everything. Their wives, sisters and daughters are not allowed to vote for president, and won't be for another nine years.

They are busy anyway. Six houses on foot, 1608 to 2115 Prairie, north to south, and at each a woman the sources tie to the house: a nurse's champion, a future detective, a diarist with a silversmith's bench in her basement, a suffragist, a fountain-builder and the street's last great lady.

Begin at the north end, with two sisters who walked into a club that had never let anyone like them in.

stops.text: 1608 Prairie, the Frank household. Henrietta Greenebaum Frank worked year after year for better nursing education at the Illinois Training School for Nurses. In 1876 she and her sister Hannah Greenebaum Solomon became the first Jewish members of the prestigious Chicago Woman's Club. Hannah went on to found the National Council of Jewish Women and was its first president. Two sisters, one door opened. A block south, a young mother is living in a house her parents built for her.

1700 Prairie, built by John and Frances Glessner for their daughter, Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898. Right now she is a society wife. Wait. Decades from now she will build eighteen tiny, perfect rooms, each one a death scene in miniature for students to solve: the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, still used to train investigators. She will help found Harvard's Department of Legal Medicine, and in 1943 she will become the first woman police captain in the United States. Her mother lives one block south, and is probably writing about her right now.

1800 Prairie, Glessner House. Frances Macbeth Glessner began a journal in 1879 and kept it for forty years, and the house museum still writes the family's story from it. She kept bees. Since 1893 her Monday Morning Reading Class has met in the library, women reading together every week through the winter and spring. And this year, 1904, she has set up a silversmith's workbench in the basement and begun making silver with her own hands. Across Eighteenth Street and down the west walk, a neighbour is fighting for something bigger.

1834 Prairie, the Fernando Jones house. Jane Grahame Jones was, in the words of the city's encyclopedia, a longtime and outspoken activist for woman suffrage; her husband's scrapbook keeps clippings on the Illinois Woman Suffrage Association from as early as 1875. She has been at it for nearly thirty years and still cannot vote. In 1913 Illinois will become the first state east of the Mississippi to let women vote for president. Keep walking south, past Twentieth Street, to a family that will give the city a fountain.

2036 Prairie, the Buckingham house, where the 1904 Blue Book lists Clarence Buckingham, philanthropist and businessman. His sister was Kate Sturges Buckingham, philanthropist and art patron. In 1927, after his death, she will give Chicago the Buckingham Fountain in his memory: twice the size of the Versailles fountain it copies, with a centre jet that throws water 150 feet into the air. One more house, and the woman who stayed after everyone else had gone.

2115 Prairie, the Kelley-Armour house. The 1904 Blue Book lists Mrs. Philip D. Armour here; the census of 1900 names her Belle, born in Ohio. Her husband, the meatpacker, died in 1901. As the great families died or moved away to suburbs like Lake Forest, she stayed on, and on. The district marker says Armour's widow was among the last residents of the street, dying here in 1927, long after most of her neighbours' houses had been sold or torn down.

legs.story: South past the 1600s. In 1904 no woman on this street can vote for president; Illinois changes that in 1913.
A block south, past the Glessner twins at 1700 and 1706, to the granite corner at Eighteenth Street.
Across Eighteenth Street and down the west walk.
To the end of the street's great row.

endings.text:
End of the walk at 2115 Prairie. Six women, six houses. A nurse's champion, a detective, a diarist, a suffragist, a fountain-builder and a widow who would not leave.

They are only the ones the sources name. Behind every one of these fronts lived maids, cooks, nurses and laundresses whose names are only in the census. Their stories are waiting too.

keepsake.title: Prairie Avenue women's roll
keepsake.text: An interpretive list of six women and their houses, not a historical document.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book's Prairie Avenue list prints the Henry L. Frank household at 1608.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., printed pp. 186-187 (PDF pp. 188-189), as the Prairie library's civic dossier reads it (chicago/prairie_1904_v1/research/civic-dossier.json).

evidence.text: Henrietta Greenebaum Frank (1608) and Ella Walker (1720) worked steadily for quality nursing education at the Illinois Training School for Nurses.
evidence.locator: The essay's paragraph on the residents' causes, which gives each woman's house number in parentheses.

evidence.text: Solomon and her sister Henrietta Frank became the first Jewish members of the prestigious Chicago Woman's Club in 1876. Hannah Greenebaum Solomon founded and served as the first president of the National Council of Jewish Women.
evidence.locator: The article's paragraphs on the Chicago Woman's Club and the National Council of Jewish Women.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book's Prairie Avenue list prints the Blewett Lee household at 1700.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., printed pp. 186-187 (PDF pp. 188-189), as the Prairie library's civic dossier reads it (chicago/prairie_1904_v1/research/civic-dossier.json).

evidence.text: 1700 and 1706 Prairie were twin townhouses John and Frances Glessner built for their two married children; the daughter Frances, married to Blewett Lee in February 1898, moved into 1700 within a few years. George Glessner photographed the pair under construction in 1901.
evidence.locator: The family page's biography of Frances Glessner Lee; the blog's 1901 construction photograph and caption.

evidence.text: Frances Glessner Lee's later work in legal medicine: the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, miniature crime scenes still used in training.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Glessner Lee.

evidence.text: She helped to establish the Department of Legal Medicine at Harvard (1931); built a series of eighteen miniature crime-scene dioramas for student analysis; and in 1943 was appointed a captain in the New Hampshire State Police, the first woman in the United States to hold such a position.
evidence.locator: The biography paragraph.

evidence.text: Frances Macbeth Glessner kept a journal from 1879 for forty years; in 1904 she set up a silversmith's workbench in the basement of the house; she kept bees; and she held the Monday Morning Reading Class in the library from 1893.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Macbeth Glessner.

evidence.text: The house museum's biographies of the family are written from its collection, Frances Glessner's journal among it.
evidence.locator: The page as a whole; the source record's note says what it is written from.

evidence.text: John and Frances Glessner lived in the house from 1 December 1887 until their deaths (1936 and 1932).
evidence.locator: HABS data pages pp. 1-2 and 9, as data/residents_1904/households/hh_glessner_john_j.json carries them.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book's Prairie Avenue list prints the Fernando Jones household at 1834.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., printed pp. 186-187 (PDF pp. 188-189), as the Prairie library's civic dossier reads it (chicago/prairie_1904_v1/research/civic-dossier.json).

evidence.text: Jane Grahame Jones (1834) fought for woman suffrage.
evidence.locator: The essay's paragraph on the residents' causes.

evidence.text: Prairie Avenue resident Jane G. Jones was a longtime and outspoken activist for women suffrage; the document is the Fernando Jones Scrapbook's clippings on the Illinois Woman Suffrage Association, 1875.
evidence.locator: The caption under the document image.

evidence.text: Illinois became the first state east of the Mississippi River to give women the right to vote for president, in 1913.
evidence.locator: The paragraph on the 1913 law.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book's Prairie Avenue list prints the E. Buckingham household and Clarence Buckingham at 2036.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., printed pp. 186-187 (PDF pp. 188-189), as the Prairie library's civic dossier reads it (chicago/prairie_1904_v1/research/civic-dossier.json).

evidence.text: Philanthropist and art patron Kate Sturges Buckingham (1858-1937) gave the funds for the fountain, dedicated to her brother, philanthropist and businessman Clarence Buckingham (1854-1913); dedicated 26 August 1927; twice the size of the Latona Basin at Versailles that inspired it; its major display sprays water 150 feet high.
evidence.locator: The page's history section.

evidence.text: The Clarence Buckingham of the 1904 listing is the Clarence Buckingham (1854-1913) the fountain honours.
evidence.reasoning: The Blue Book lists a Clarence Buckingham in the E. Buckingham household of 2036 Prairie; the fountain honours a Chicago philanthropist and businessman of that name living in 1904 (1854-1913). Same name, same city, same years; no source read here states the identity in words.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book's Prairie Avenue list prints Mrs. Philip D. Armour at 2115.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., printed pp. 186-187 (PDF pp. 188-189), as the Prairie library's civic dossier reads it (chicago/prairie_1904_v1/research/civic-dossier.json).

evidence.text: David Kelley-Philip D. Armour Residence: for nearly 50 years the home of the family of meatpacker Philip D. Armour; Armour's widow was among the last residents of the street, dying here in 1927.
evidence.locator: The 2115 S. Prairie Avenue entry.

evidence.text: After the 1890s many of the leading Prairie Avenue families died or moved to suburbs such as Lake Forest.
evidence.locator: The essay's closing paragraph on the street's decline.

evidence.text: The route, its order, its spring morning, its reading times, its keepsake and its framing are modern interpretation; no historical visit, conversation or occupant on a day in 1904 is asserted.
The 1900 census lists Belle O. Armour at 2115 Prairie as the wife of the household, born in Ohio.
evidence.locator: ED 40, sheet 14B, line 69, leaf n821, as data/residents_1904/households/hh_armour_mrs_philip_d.json reads it.
